transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

Well, I came in because there’s been… there’s something going on with the environmental modeling contract I’m working on. I know it sounds like office politics, but it’s more than that. The people involved have been tracking my revisions, watching what I change, and somehow these errors keep showing up in the datasets after I’ve handled them.

My wife says it’s probably version-control mistakes, and the junior analysts say the same thing, but I’ve worked with data a long time. You can tell when something is just a merge issue versus when it’s placed there. It makes me look like I can’t lead the work, which is convenient for certain people. And I used to teach myself Fortran off manuals, so I’m not exactly careless with files—anyway, that’s why I’m here, I guess.
Do you feel that people are deliberately trying to harm your reputation or sabotage your work, even if there’s no clear evidence that they are?

Yes, I do. I mean, I can’t hand you a signed memo or anything, but it’s… it’s too patterned to be random. On that environmental modeling contract, they’ve been watching my revisions, and then these little errors appear in the datasets after I’ve worked on them, the kind that make me look sloppy or like I shouldn’t be leading it.

My wife keeps saying it’s probably version-control issues, and the junior analysts say that too, but they didn’t spend years working through code and models the way I did. I know what a normal mistake looks like. This feels placed. And of course, if I look incompetent, that benefits certain people.
Outside of your work situation, do you ever feel that people in general are trying to harm you or mislead you in other areas of your life?

Mostly it’s the contract. That’s where it’s clearest. I mean, I’m not walking around thinking every cashier or neighbor is involved or anything… but once you see how people can mislead you in one place, it makes you more careful.

With this environmental modeling work, though, I’m pretty sure they’ve been tracking my revisions and planting little errors in the datasets after I touch them. My wife says, “It’s version control,” and the junior analysts say the same thing, but that feels too convenient. I’ve worked with models and code long enough to know when something’s just a mistake versus when it’s meant to make me look like I can’t lead the work.

I used to spend hours with manuals figuring things out—Fortran, old numerical routines, all that—so it’s not like I’m careless. Sorry, I know you asked outside of work. I guess… mostly no, not in general. But at work, yes, very much.
Have you ever experienced any strange or unusual thoughts, such as hearing voices or believing things that others don't seem to understand, outside of the issues you're having at work?

I don’t know… I mean, hearing voices, no, not like that. Not that I’ve noticed. People say “strange thoughts,” but that can mean a lot of things, right? When I was younger I used to get very wrapped up in problems—math problems, code, manuals, that sort of thing—and I’d be thinking about them for hours, but that’s not the same as hearing something.

Outside of work, I can’t really point to anything like that. It’s more that the work situation has been… well, it has a structure to it. But no, I don’t think I’ve had voices or anything like that outside of the contract stuff.
Have you ever had beliefs or ideas that others around you don’t seem to share or understand, even when you’ve tried to explain them?

Yes… I think that’s basically why I’m here. I’ve tried to explain it to my wife, and to the junior analysts too, but they keep saying it’s version-control mistakes, like files getting crossed or someone using the wrong dataset. But that doesn’t fit with what I’m seeing.

On that environmental modeling contract, after I make revisions, these little errors show up in the data—small enough that someone could say, “Oh, that’s just a mistake,” but they’re placed in a way that makes me look like I can’t manage the work. And I’ve worked with models and datasets for a long time, back when you had to really understand the routines, not just click through software, so I know the difference between ordinary sloppiness and something that’s being done to undermine you.

So, yes, other people don’t seem to understand it, or they don’t want to. My wife says I’m reading too much into it, but I’m pretty sure my revisions are being tracked and the errors are being planted after I touch the files.
Have you ever had any beliefs or suspicions that are completely unrelated to your work situation, that others don’t seem to understand or agree with, even when you’ve tried to explain them clearly?

Completely unrelated to work? I don’t think so, not really. I mean, I get careful about things, sure, but the thing that brought me here is the contract.

That’s where it’s obvious to me—the environmental modeling work. I make revisions, and then these little errors appear in the datasets afterward, in ways that point back at me, like I can’t lead the project. My wife says it’s version-control mistakes, and the junior analysts say the same thing, but… I’ve worked with this kind of material long enough to know when something doesn’t add up.

So outside of that, no, I can’t think of some separate belief like that. It’s mainly this work situation.
Have you ever had any ideas or beliefs that you know are unusual, that no one else seems to share, and that you haven't been able to let go of, even if they don’t have to do with your job?

I mean… unusual to other people, yes, I guess. I don’t think of it as “unusual” exactly, because when you’ve worked with datasets long enough you can see patterns other people miss. It’s like—years ago, before all these tools got so automated, you had to know what the numbers were doing, not just trust the screen.

But the thing I can’t really let go of is the contract. The environmental modeling one. I’m pretty sure my revisions are being tracked, and then errors are getting planted in the datasets after I touch them, so it looks like I can’t lead the work. My wife says it’s just version-control problems, and the junior analysts say the same kind of thing, but that explanation doesn’t fit right to me. It keeps lining up too neatly against me.
Have you ever believed something that you know is not based in reality, something that you realize other people would find hard to believe, even aside from the issues at work?

Not based in reality… I don’t know if I’d put it that way. I know my wife would say it isn’t realistic, and the junior analysts act like I’m making connections that aren’t there.

But I’m here because of that contract, really. The environmental modeling one. I’ll make revisions, and then afterward these errors turn up in the datasets—small things, but in just the wrong places, like they’re meant to point back to me and make it seem like I can’t lead the work. And people keep saying, “Oh, it’s version-control mistakes,” but I’ve been around this kind of work long enough to know when something is off.

Aside from work… I don’t know. That’s the thing that keeps sticking in my mind. I realize other people find it hard to believe, but I don’t feel like I can just dismiss it.

Have you ever had any beliefs or suspicions that aren’t related to your work situation, that you know are not shared by others, but you still feel certain are true even though there may not be clear proof?

Not really outside work, no. I keep coming back to the same thing, the modeling contract. I know you’re asking “not related to work,” but that’s where it is for me.

I’m pretty sure people on that environmental project have been tracking my revisions. I’ll change something, and then later errors show up in the datasets, little ones, but placed so it reflects badly on me—like I’m not capable of leading it. My wife says it’s probably version-control mistakes, and the junior analysts say that too, but… I’ve used these systems for years. It doesn’t feel random. It feels like it’s being done to make me look incompetent.
Are there times when you believe something strongly, even though you know others don't share that belief and there's no clear proof to support it?

Yeah… I mean, that’s probably what everyone would call it. I don’t have proof in the way you’d put in a report, with timestamps and a clean audit trail—though, you know, those systems never capture everything anyway. I used to tell people that when we were doing older modeling runs, before the software got so… polished.

But yes, I believe it pretty strongly. The people on that environmental modeling contract, I’m pretty sure they’ve been tracking my revisions and then planting errors in the datasets after I touch them. Not huge errors, little ones, the kind that make it look like I don’t know what I’m doing or can’t lead the work. My wife says it’s version-control mistakes, and the junior analysts say the same thing, but that just feels too convenient to me. I know they don’t see it the way I do, but I can’t shake it.
Are there times when you believe something is definitely true, even though you know most people would say there’s no way to prove it and it doesn’t make sense to them?

Yes. I mean… yes, that’s why I’m sitting here, really. It’s the contract, the environmental modeling one. I know my wife says it doesn’t make sense, and the younger analysts keep saying it’s just version-control problems, but I don’t buy that.

I’m pretty sure they’ve been watching my revisions and then putting errors into the datasets after I work on them. Small errors, not obvious ones—things that make it look like I can’t manage the project or lead the work. And I know people want proof, like a neat audit trail, but those systems don’t show everything. I’ve worked with data long enough to know when something isn’t just a mistake.

opening_question.question: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient exhibits persistent, non-bizarre delusions centered around a specific theme—specifically, that colleagues are deliberately tracking their work and planting errors to undermine their professional competence. There is no evidence of prominent hallucinations, disorganized speech, or grossly disorganized or catatonic behavior. The delusional theme is non-paranoid in nature, focused on a perceived professional sabotage, and has persisted for an extended period, consistent with Delusional Disorder.
